item.title: Vicksburg police investigate shots fired into home - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
VICKSBURG – Vicksburg police are investigating after gunfire struck a home Wednesday night.

According to the Vicksburg Police Department, officers responded May 27 to the 100 block of Elizabeth Circle in reference to a shots-fired call.

During the investigation, officers determined that at least one projectile struck the residence, entered the home and traveled through two separate bedroom walls.

No injuries were reported. The investigation remains ongoing. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Vicksburg Police Department or Crime Stoppers at 601-355-TIPS (8477).

item.title: Two gang members sentenced in ATM jackpotting scheme, await deportation - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
Two Venezuelan Tren de Aragua gang members have been sentenced for conspiracy to commit bank fraud in connection with an ATM jackpotting scheme, Attorney General Lynn Fitch announced.

According to Fitch’s office, Darrin Moises Daza-Segura and Winder Alexander Canelon-Tiapa traveled throughout Mississippi reprogramming bank ATMs to dispense large amounts of cash. The crime is commonly known as ATM jackpotting.

Officials said disrupting the group prevented nearly $180,000 in potential fraud losses.

“Thanks to the diligent work of our Cyber Fraud Task Force, we were able to prevent nearly $180,000 in losses, deprive TdA gang members of money to fund their crimes, and set up the deportation of two criminal illegal aliens,” Fitch said. “We are proud to stand with our local, state, and federal partners to stop this criminal scheme in its tracks.”

United States District Judge Michael P. Mills sentenced both men to 10 months in the custody of the Federal Bureau of Prisons, followed by three years of supervised release. They were also ordered to pay $47,250 in restitution to the affected banks.

Fitch’s office said both men entered the country illegally and will be subject to deportation after they are released from prison.

The case was investigated by the Mississippi Attorney General’s Office, with assistance from the Madison Police Department, Raymond Police Department, Tupelo Police Department, Amory Police Department, Duncanville Police Department in Texas and St. George Police Department in Utah. It was prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Mississippi.

Fitch created the Mississippi Cyber Fraud Task Force in partnership with the U.S. Secret Service in 2021.

item.title: Tippah County Lake to reopen for fishing, boating after storm cleanup - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
TIPPAH COUNTY – Tippah County Lake in Ripley will reopen Saturday, May 30, for fishing and boating, according to the Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks.

MDWFP said crews have been working to clean and restore the area following damage from Winter Storm Fern in January.

The lake had been temporarily closed because of ongoing cleanup efforts and storm debris removal.

While fishing and boating will resume Saturday, the campground will remain closed as repairs and debris cleanup continue.

MDWFP said it will notify the public once the campground reopens. More information about Tippah County Lake is available at mdwfp.com.

item.title: Summer Stock Up food drive aims to fill Mississippi Food Network shelves for summer kids' programs - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON — Two metro-area Kroger stores will become collection points Friday for the Summer Stock Up food drive, a one-day effort to restock the Mississippi Food Network ahead of the summer months when school meal programs go dark for thousands of children.

The drive runs from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. Friday, June 5, at the Kroger at the Promenade in Flowood and the Kroger off Highway 51 in Madison. Organizers say donors can drop off food or hand cash through a car window without leaving their vehicles. Shoppers entering either store will be greeted with a list of the most-needed items and asked to add a few to their carts.

The drive partners the Mississippi Food Network with the Mississippi Farm Bureau Federation’s Foundation for Agriculture, along with radio partners US96.3, 93.5 The Legend, Y101, Rock 93.1 and Mix 98.7, and Darkhorse Press. The goal is to fill the large bulk containers staged in the parking lots and stock the shelves for the food bank’s summer programs for children. Each receptacle holds roughly 1,000 pounds of food, enough to provide about 833 meals.

The need is steep. Mississippi has the highest rate of food insecurity in the nation. In the Mississippi Food Network’s service area, roughly one in five people, or about 345,000 Mississippians, are food insecure, and 26.5 percent of children, or one in four, go to bed hungry.

The summer months hit children hardest. The food bank’s Kids Café and Summer Food Service Programs provide hot meals and healthy snacks to children when school is out of session and the free and reduced-price meals many families rely on are unavailable.

Most-needed items include canned meats such as tuna, chili, beef stew, Spam, chicken, Vienna sausage and chicken and dumplings, along with peanut butter, canned fruit, canned vegetables, canned soups, boxed stuffing mix, boxed mashed or scalloped potatoes, boxed macaroni and cheese, ramen noodles, and cake mixes and icing.

Donors who prefer to give money can do so at the drive or online at msfoodnet.org. Every $10 donation provides 60 meals; a $100 gift provides 600. The food bank says every dollar donated provides six meals, and 95 cents of every dollar goes directly to its programs.

The Mississippi Food Network has fed Mississippians since 1984, distributing more than 2.3 million pounds of food each month through 430 member agencies and feeding more than 163,000 people monthly, or nearly 2 million people a year. Monetary donations can also be mailed to Mississippi Food Network, P.O. Box 411, Jackson, MS 39205.

item.title: Substitute teacher at Hernando High School arrested on child pornography charge - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
HERNANDO – A substitute teacher at Hernando High School has been arrested and charged with one count of child pornography.

According to the DeSoto County District Attorney’s Office, 69-year-old Preston Ivan Lewis was arrested following an investigation by local law enforcement.

Officials said Lewis served as a substitute Spanish teacher at Hernando High School. The district attorney’s office said Lewis was not an employee of the DeSoto County School District and was employed through Kelly Services, a third-party staffing company that provides substitute personnel to school districts.

District Attorney Matthew Barton said the investigation remains ongoing and that authorities are continuing to review digital evidence.

“We have heard the concerns from parents and want you all to know that this is an ongoing investigation, and information continues to come in while we sift through the digital evidence already collected,” Barton said. “All individuals who can be identified so far have been contacted. We will immediately contact victims if additional people are identified.”

Barton also praised the DeSoto County School District and law enforcement for their response.

“The DeSoto County School District’s response was immediate and exemplary,” Barton said. “Their swift action helped protect our children, and I thank the district and law enforcement for their hard work in this case involving a depraved individual.”

Authorities said additional information will be released when appropriate and when doing so will not compromise the ongoing investigation.

item.title: STEPPING UP TO SERVE: Columbus businesses donate water to help keep firefighters hydrated this summer - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
COLUMBUS – Local businesses are stepping up to help keep Columbus firefighters hydrated as summer temperatures rise.

The Columbus Fire and Rescue Department thanked Dan Price and the team at Food Giant, along with Benton and Military Hardware, for donating bottled water to support firefighters during the hot summer months.

Fire officials said Mississippi heat can take a toll on first responders as they train, respond to medical calls, work fires and spend long hours on emergency scenes.

The department said something as simple as cold bottled water can make a big difference for the men and women serving the community.

“We truly appreciate businesses and citizens who continue to support Columbus, MS Fire and Rescue Department and stand behind their first responders,” the department said. “Support like this does not go unnoticed.”

Anyone who would like to help support firefighters this summer may donate bottled water or sports drinks. Donations can be dropped off at Columbus Fire and Rescue Station 1, located at 201 7th St. S. in Columbus.

The department thanked Food Giant and Military Hardware for their generosity and continued community support.

item.title: Star Volunteer Fire Department marks 50 years with BBQ fundraiser June 20 - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
STAR — For half a century, the volunteers of the Star Volunteer Fire Department have answered the call in Rankin County.

The department will host its 50th Annual BBQ Fundraiser beginning at 10 a.m. at Star Baptist Church’s CLC parking lot in Star, serving drive-thru style until sold out. Chicken and hamburger plates are $10 each and include baked beans, coleslaw, bread and a drink.

Fire Chief Jackie Squires said the event is about more than a meal.

“Come buy a plate, stop by and say hi, show a little support,” Squires said on Facebook. “Your hometown crews are ready and willing to not only serve you a hot meal but to serve you in your emergency. All monies raised goes to valuable equipment to help us on any call.”

Proceeds will go toward the purchase of lifesaving equipment for the department, which has served the Star community since 1976. All donations are welcomed in addition to plate sales.

The Star Volunteer Fire Department is an all-volunteer organization operating under the motto “Neighbors Helping Neighbors.

Squires said the department is grateful for the community support that has sustained it through 50 years.

All donations are welcomed.

item.title: Oxford police make arrests in multistate burglary case involving $140,000 in stolen jewelry - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
OXFORD – Two men have been arrested in connection with a multistate burglary investigation that began after more than $140,000 worth of jewelry was stolen from an Oxford home, police said.

According to the Oxford Police Department, officers responded May 16 to a residence on St. Andrews Road in reference to a burglary. After officers secured the area, investigators responded to the scene.

Investigators said they found the point of entry and recovered footprints and a partial fingerprint inside the home. They also obtained surveillance video from the area, which showed multiple people entering a vehicle parked nearby that did not belong to anyone living in the area. Neighbors had reported the vehicle as suspicious, police said.

Investigators used traffic cameras and tag readers to track the vehicle. Police said the vehicle had entered Oxford with a different license plate, leading investigators to expand their search into other states.

Oxford investigators contacted agencies in Alabama and learned those agencies were investigating similar burglaries. Police said the vehicle was later spotted in Arkansas, Missouri and Illinois.

OPD investigators tracked the vehicle to an area in Missouri and helped guide the Missouri Highway Patrol to the vehicle. The vehicle was stopped, and the suspects were arrested after a foot pursuit.

Fabian Ignacio Navarro-Aliaga, 27, and Marcelo Alejandro Telechea-Droguett, 36, both of Chile, were arrested and charged by Oxford police with burglary, forced entry. Police said both men were also issued federal charges, and immigration detainers were placed on them.

Jewelry, firearms and other stolen items have been recovered and are being identified by their owners.

The Oxford Police Department thanked the Missouri Highway Patrol, Chicago Police Department and Department of Homeland Security for assisting in the case.

Police said the investigation remains ongoing, and more charges are pending in several other states.

item.title: Ocean Springs police seek man wanted for felony embezzlement - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
OCEAN SPRINGS – Authorities are asking for the public’s help finding a man wanted on a felony embezzlement charge.

According to Mississippi Coast Crime Stoppers, Joshua “Josh” Sumrall is wanted by the Ocean Springs Police Department for felony embezzlement of money from a former employer.

Sumrall’s last known address was in Vancleave, officials said.

item.title: MSU’s Berry, White join elite class of national Astronaut Scholars - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Special to Darkhorse Press
item.description:
STARKVILLE — Two Bulldog engineering majors have earned the prestigious title of Astronaut Scholar, a recognition reserved for the best and brightest science-focused undergraduates in the country.

Madelyn “Sloan” Berry of Brandon and India “Alex” White of Saltillo are Mississippi State’s latest recipients of the nationally renowned Astronaut Scholarship. They are among only 79 students nationwide receiving up to $15,000 and joining the national Astronaut Scholarship Foundation’s lifelong network of professional mentors and peer researchers.

Both Berry and White are members of MSU’s Judy and Bobby Shackouls Honors College, and White was named a national Barry Goldwater Scholar this spring.

Berry, a senior aerospace engineering major with a 4.0 GPA, is a Louis A. Hurst Jr. Presidential Endowed Scholarship recipient at MSU who plans to research composites and help build the next generation of high-speed aircraft after college. As an undergraduate, she served as a researcher at MSU’s Aerostructures for Hypersonic Flight Research Laboratory and the university’s Remote Sensing Payload Research and Development program. Berry will spend this summer with the U.S. Department of Defense as an engineering analyst intern. Her diverse list of extracurricular activities includes serving as president of the CubeSat at MSU satellite design team, treasurer of the MSU chapter of the Society for the Advancement of Material and Process Engineering and leading the Famous Maroon Band piccolo section, among others.

White, a senior biomedical engineering major also with a 4.0 GPA, is an MSU Luckyday Scholar who plans to lead her own lab, spearheading research and teaching in a hospital setting, helping advance breast cancer treatment options. White boasts research experience with MSU’s Priddy Lab and Neural Engineering Research Division, the University of Alabama at Birmingham’s Advanced Medical Imaging Research Division and the University of Mississippi’s A.R.I.S.E program. She was recently accepted into the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center’s summer research program, where she will work in the Department of Epigenetics and Molecular Carcinogenesis. White previously served as the secretary for MSU’s Unified Sports program and is a Tau Beta Pi member, Brickfire Project mentor, Luckyday Scholars Program mentor and Spring Preview Day panelist.

Juniors and seniors intending to pursue research or advance their field upon completion of their final degrees are eligible for the Astronaut Scholarship. They are selected for their initiative, creativity and excellence in their chosen field. In addition to receiving a financial award, they enjoy networking and mentoring opportunities with astronauts, alumni and industry leaders; participation in the Michael Collins Family Professional Development Program; and a paid trip to attend ASF’s Innovators Week and Gala in Houston, Texas, which provides an opportunity for the scholars to present their research at a technical conference.

MSU’s Office of Prestigious External Scholarships connects students to competitive scholarships and fellowships and assists with their applications. Visit www.honors.msstate.edu/initiatives/office-prestigious-external-scholarships for more information.

The Shackouls Honors College is online at www.honors.msstate.edu .

item.title: Mississippi Supreme Court refuses to hear appeal of Tate County man convicted in girlfriend's shooting death - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON — The Mississippi Supreme Court has declined to take up the case of a Tate County man convicted in the 2022 shooting death of his girlfriend, ending his bid to overturn the conviction.

The court denied Demarcus Wooten’s petition for writ of certiorari May 21, with all justices in agreement. The order closes out appellate review after the Mississippi Court of Appeals unanimously affirmed his conviction and sentence in October 2025.

Wooten was convicted of manslaughter in Tate County Circuit Court following a November 2023 trial and sentenced to 20 years in the custody of the Mississippi Department of Corrections. He had been indicted on first-degree murder in the death of LaRhonda Jackson.

Jackson was shot in the chest Feb. 13, 2022, during a car ride with Wooten and her 2-year-old son. Wooten told investigators the shooting was accidental, saying Jackson grabbed his gun from the center console and the weapon discharged during a struggle before he crashed his SUV into a tree.

Prosecutors presented forensic evidence showing the bullet traveled front to back and downward, and a law enforcement witness testified that it would have been difficult for Jackson to access the gun given its location in the console. The jury found Wooten guilty of the lesser charge of manslaughter.

On appeal, Wooten argued the trial court wrongly excluded his defense expert witness, improperly allowed a law enforcement officer to offer opinions about his relationship with Jackson, and gave a misleading jury instruction. The Court of Appeals found no reversible error in any of those claims.

The exclusion of the defense expert stemmed from a months-long dispute over discovery materials and a series of missed deadlines. Circuit Court Judge James McClure III barred the expert after the defense failed to produce a report despite multiple extensions and after defense counsel missed a status conference.

With the Supreme Court’s denial, Wooten’s conviction and 20-year sentence stand.

item.title: Jones County deputies respond to shooting in Glade community - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
GLADE – Jones County deputies responded Thursday afternoon to a shots fired call after a man was reportedly struck by gunfire at a home on Magnolia Tree Road in the Glade community.

item.title: Byram Police Department brings back youth camp that's changed dozens of lives - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
HOW TO GET INVOLVED:

WHEN: Thursdays and Fridays from June 4 through July 10 WHAT TIME: Drop-off is at 4 p.m., Camp is from 4:30-8:15 p.m. WHERE TO REGISTER: Byram Police Department or Byram City Hall (in person, please) COST: $25 for 11 and up, $15 for 10 and under WHERE IS CAMP: Byram Middle School CONTACT: Elroy Winding at 601-927-9943 or Erma Johnson at 601-918-6369

BYRAM — It started with a teenager who loved basketball, a patrol officer who saw his potential, and a crime that couldn’t be undone.

That was the beginning of the Blue Dawgs Youth Camp, and it’s why Detective Judson Magloire will spend another summer after two years off pouring his off-duty hours into keeping kids off the streets.

“I felt like if I was still on patrol, I would have had more time to interact with him,” Magloire said of the young man who inspired the program, a kid he’d met at 13, shot hoops with on neighborhood courts and watched slide into trouble despite his talent. “I felt like it would have prevented him from committing the crime that he committed.”

The young man is still in prison. He calls Magloire, and they write letters.

“The first letter, I was so hurt, it took me a while to actually talk to him,” Magloire said. “He basically apologized. He regretted what he did and realized everything that I was trying to teach him.”

Magloire says the teen told him that he gets out, he wants to come speak to the kids.

The Blue Dawgs Youth Camp begins

It broke his heart.

Magloire took his grief to his command staff, pitched a structured summer program for Byram-area youth, and got a green light. The Blue Dawgs Youth Camp was born.

It started in 2022, and went strong through 2023, but then Magloire changed departments.

Now back in its third year after those two years off, the camp runs evenings on Thursdays and Fridays 6 p.m. to around 9 p.m. at Byram Middle School, timed deliberately to compete with the hours when juvenile crime spikes. The 2026 session runs June 4 through July 10, and it is open to any youth in the Byram-Hinds County area, free of charge.

The results have been striking. During the summers the program has run, youth-related crime in Byram dropped by roughly 50 percent. In the 2023 session, not a single Byram resident youth was arrested on a misdemeanor or violent charge for the duration of the camp.

“The feeling was very rewarding and really unreal,” Magloire said. “The goal was to just help one youth versus all of them. It was really tremendous.”

Everybody wins

Byram Chief Kevin Turner said the stakes couldn’t be clearer.

Drawing on the book of Isaiah, the chief pointed to a passage describing how Hell enlarges itself to receive more souls as more arrive, and he said crime feels the same sometimes.

“When you look at the community, not just us but just in the metro area, they’re closing schools but they’re expanding jails,” Turner said. “It seems like we’re preparing for more crime and we’re not doing as much to prevent it as we are preparing for it to happen.”

The camp, he said, is the department’s answer to that math.

“Instead of us being police officers and waiting on them to mess up so we can punish, we talk more about punish the behavior and not enough about how to deter it,” Turner said. “We’re coming out of our comfort zone, meeting them where they are to keep them from taking that road.”

The program’s reach has inspired programs well beyond Byram. After Blue Dawgs launched, the Jackson Police Department restarted its own PALS summer program. Hinds County followed with its Warriors program. And Judge Hicks of Hinds County Youth Court began ordering juvenile offenders to complete the Blue Dawgs program as a condition of having their charges dropped.

“After we did that, JPD started their summer program again,” Assistant Chief Derrick Jordan said. “It sparked Hinds County to start their Warriors program. And not only that, any kid that got in trouble — one of their stipulations would be that they have to attend our program. If they completed the summer program and got their certificate, their charges would be dropped.”

What to expect

Past camps have brought in SWAT teams, youth court and circuit court judges, and an MHP helicopter that landed on-site, which is a moment Magloire still talks about. The kids were in awe, and some were inspired. In fact, a camper who wanted to be an aviation mechanic asked questions of the crew, but already he knew every answer.

Parents have come away changed, too. At one session, families learned that a juvenile who brandishes a BB gun while implying it’s real has committed a violent crime under Mississippi law, a fact that stunned the room.

“Even though it was a BB gun and not a real gun?” parents asked. Yes, Magloire told them. And that’s prison time.

Officers have given as much as the kids. Patrol officers, warrant officers and their families all volunteered. Officer Washington once refereed a kickball game in his bulletproof vest, tactical helmet and a whistle.

Magloire’s own children have been involved in the camp. This year, his son will manage the game room.

“We had a great time,” Magloire said. “And I’m glad we’re doing the program again.”

The camp is free and open to all youth in the Byram-Hinds County area. Volunteers who can pass a background check are also welcome to participate. For more information, contact the Byram Police Department.

item.title: Two arrested after stolen truck, trailers lead to multiple pursuits across Mississippi, Alabama - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
GEORGE COUNTY – Two people have been arrested following multiple theft investigations and vehicle pursuits involving stolen property in George County and Mobile County, Alabama.

According to the George County Sheriff’s Office, deputies were investigating a possible stolen vehicle May 24 in the Agricola area of George County when they saw the vehicle being driven by Charles Mott. Deputies attempted to stop the vehicle for traffic violations, but the vehicle fled into Alabama.

A few hours later, Mobile County deputies saw the vehicle and attempted a traffic stop, which led to another pursuit. Authorities said the pursuit continued until the vehicle came back into Greene County, Mississippi, where it ended. The vehicle was not recovered at that time.

On May 26, the George County Sheriff’s Office received a report of a stolen travel trailer from the Rocky Creek area. Investigators learned the trailer was at Mott’s property in Agricola. Investigators went to the property and confirmed through the VIN that it was the stolen trailer from Rocky Creek.

While investigators were recovering the stolen camper trailer, other George County deputies saw the previously stolen truck, which had been painted a different color, towing a large flatbed trailer in the Howell area of George County. Authorities said Mott was driving the vehicle, and Stephanie Valentine was also inside.

Deputies attempted another traffic stop, but the suspects again fled into Mobile County, Alabama. Mobile County authorities later saw the vehicle and attempted a traffic stop, which led to another pursuit. Mobile County deputies were ultimately able to stop the vehicle and arrest Mott and Valentine without further incident.

Both are being held at the Mobile County Metro Jail.

Mott is facing charges in Mobile County, Alabama, including first-degree robbery, first-degree receiving stolen property, felony attempt to elude, three counts of first-degree criminal mischief, three counts of second-degree assault and fugitive from justice in Mississippi.

Valentine is facing charges in Mobile County, including first-degree robbery, second-degree possession of marijuana, possession of drug paraphernalia, second-degree elder abuse and fugitive from justice in Mississippi.

On May 27, the George County Sheriff’s Office received a report of a stolen flatbed trailer from the Shipman area. Deputies identified the trailer as the same one being towed by Mott during the May 26 pursuit.

On May 28, the George County Criminal Investigation Division received information about the trailer’s location in the Semmes, Alabama, area. The trailer has since been recovered.

The George County Sheriff’s Office has placed holds on Mott for motor vehicle theft, grand larceny of a camper trailer, grand larceny of a flatbed trailer and felony fleeing.

Valentine has holds for grand larceny of a camper trailer and grand larceny of a flatbed trailer.

“These individuals demonstrated a blatant disregard for the law and the safety of others by repeatedly fleeing from law enforcement,” Sheriff Mitchell Mixon said. “Let this serve as a reminder that the George County Sheriff’s Office will continue pressing forward to hold accountable those who commit crimes in our community, regardless of where they attempt to flee.”

Mixon commended George County deputies, investigators and dispatchers, along with the Mobile County Sheriff’s Office, for helping apprehend the suspects and recover the stolen property.

All suspects are presumed innocent until proven guilty.

item.title: Tunica Humane Society issues warning about leaving children and pets in vehicles - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
TUNICA COUNTY – The Tunica Humane Society is warning the public about the dangers of leaving pets unattended inside vehicles as temperatures continue to rise.

In a recent social media post, the organization stressed that temperatures inside a vehicle can increase rapidly and become deadly in a matter of minutes.

According to the post, if the outside temperature is 85 degrees, the temperature inside a vehicle can climb to 104 degrees within 10 minutes.

The humane society urged the public to never leave children or pets inside a parked vehicle, even for a short trip into a store.

Officials said the risk increases the longer a person or animal remains inside the vehicle.

item.title: "He was an angel:" JPD officer searches for cop who changed her life's course - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON — Captain Barbara Folsom-McNeal is a cop looking for an unknown man. He’s not a suspect. He’s not a witness. He’s another officer, he’s the reason she’s alive, and she’s running out of time to tell him so.

An Angel

Folsom-McNeal was 11 years old in the early 1980s, standing at a kitchen sink on Willow Street, praying to die.

She doesn’t remember if she was crying. She remembers washing dishes after taking a severe beating from a grief-stricken mother. She remembers her sleeves were rolled up. She remembers asking God to take her.

Then someone started beating on the door.

Folsom-McNeal, now a captain in the Jackson Police Department’s Internal Affairs Division with 24 years on the force, has spent years trying to find the officer who came to her home on that day. She told the hosts of the Investigation: Homicide podcast that remembers him as tall, but she was small. She knows he was white, and using her experience now to reflect on that day, she’s pretty sure he was a veteran JPD officer.

He worked what is now Precinct 2. She doesn’t know his name. She barely remembers his face after four decades. But she remembers exactly what he did: He saw her.

“Only thing I could say — he was an angel,” she said during a recent episode of the Investigation: Homicide podcast. “He was an angel.”

Grief changed everything

Folsom-McNeal grew up the oldest of six children in a Jackson home that changed after a devastating family tragedy when she was 8. Her brother was struck by a car in front of their home. He never regained consciousness. His heart beat for three days after his mind died, and before his body gave up. Part of their mother died with him.

Her mother’s grief, Folsom-McNeal says carefully, was overwhelming in a way that reshaped their home. She is clear that she does not want her mother remembered harshly — she’s gone now, and Folsom-McNeal has spent years making peace with a complicated love.

“I’m not saying what she did was right,” she said. “But as an adult, I kind of understand that somebody should have stepped in and said she needs some additional help.”

What Folsom-McNeal will say is that by the time she was 11 or 12, she had stopped wanting to be here. She was carrying more than any child should carry. There was grief she couldn’t understand, responsibility for her siblings, and actual physical pain she hid beneath her clothes.

“Come here”

On the night the police came to Willow Street, called by her father after her brother arrived at his home breathless, two officers were at the door, going back and forth with her mother.

A third stood back, watching. Folsom-McNeal, from inside the house, was peeking around a corner, watching him.

“He was allowing them to handle it before he stepped in,” she said. “And he looked at me. He saw me. He was like, ‘Come here.'”

She walked to him. He knelt down. He took both her hands in his.

Her sleeves were still rolled up, and the wounds from that afternoon were exposed. She had spent so long hiding the things that happened to her, but she hadn’t had time to think about it. And he saw her… clearly.

“They had to hold him back,” she said quietly, “because he lost it.”

He carried her to JPD headquarters. He sat her on a desk in a detective’s office. “Look what she did to that baby,” she remembers him saying.

That night, the children were removed from the home.

“I owe him my life,” Folsom-McNeal said. “Because at that time, I really didn’t want to live anymore.”

His legacy

She went on to become the thing he was to her.

In January 2002, she entered the JPD academy. She worked patrol in Precinct 4, became a quality-of-life officer, then a detective, then a sergeant, then a lieutenant. Today she commands the Internal Affairs Division as a captain, and at least once a week she walks into JPD Headquarters, the very building where that officer took her years ago and gave her a reason to live.

Twenty-four years of showing up at doors. Twenty-four years of looking past the surface of a scene to see who else might be standing in the background, hoping someone notices.

“Did I help somebody?” she asks herself. “Did I do something? Because I got to give back and pay it forward, because this person did it for me.”

She is eligible to retire, but she isn’t ready. But she is aware of the clock ticking not just on her career, but on the search.

She has asked questions through the years. She has stared at old composites at the JPD academy, hoping for a spark of recognition. She has looked up her old home on Google Maps, trying to ignite a memory she could act on. She finally decided after her birthday last week to launch a real search.

The officer, if he is still living, would be in his late 60s or older. He may be long retired. He may not remember the call at all. He may not know that the small girl he carried downtown that night went on to spend the next quarter century doing exactly what he did: walking into hard situations, looking past the noise, finding the next person who needed to be found. Who needed to be saved.

“I cannot leave my career at this point without knowing him and knowing who he is,” she said. “At least I want to give honor to the person that made it possible for me to be here today.”

Someone knows him

If you worked JPD in the late 1980s, or know someone who did, and you have any information about a tall, white senior officer who worked the Willow Street area in what is now Precinct 2, contact Therese Apel at [email protected] or reach out to Folsom-McNeal directly. Any information helps narrow down who he might be.

Even if he isn’t still alive, Folsom-McNeal says, she just wants his family to know what he did for her, and though she won’t say it in as many words, what her friends and coworkers would say she’s spent every day of the last 24 years doing for others in return.

“And even if he’s no longer with us or anything, at least I could tell if he had some children or somebody that can know what he did for me,” she said.

item.title: Former Olive Branch teacher sentenced to 25 years in child exploitation case - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
OLIVE BRANCH – Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch announced that a former Olive Branch teacher and preacher has been sentenced in a child exploitation case stemming from a 2023 undercover operation.

Former Olive Branch Pastor/Teacher Charged With Child Exploitation

According to the Attorney General’s Office, 32-year-old Kyle Michael Hilleary of Olive Branch was convicted on one count of child exploitation following a jury trial. The case was investigated and prosecuted by the Mississippi Attorney General’s Office with assistance from the Olive Branch Police Department. Authorities said the investigation originated from “Operation Toil and Trouble,” an undercover operation conducted in 2023.

On May 26, 2026, 23rd Circuit Court Judge Celeste Wilson sentenced Hilleary to 35 years, with 25 years to serve day-for-day without the possibility of parole in the custody of the Mississippi Department of Corrections. He was also sentenced to five years of probation.

In addition, Hilleary was ordered to pay $1,000 to the Victims of Human Trafficking and Commercial Sexual Exploitation Fund and $1,000 to the Mississippi Children’s Trust Fund. He is also required to register as a sex offender.

“These crimes rob a child of their innocence and the images can cause a lifetime of trauma, re-victimizing the child over and over again,” Attorney General Lynn Fitch said in a statement. “And when the perpetrator is someone in a position of authority, they violate a covenant with the parents who entrusted them with their children. We will not tolerate such abuse.”

Officials encouraged anyone with information about online child sexual exploitation to contact the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children at 1-800-843-5678 or submit a report online at cybertipline.org.

item.title: Florida men sentenced in Madison Burn Boot Camp burglary spree - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
MADISON — Two Florida men have been sentenced to decades in prison for their roles in a series of vehicle burglaries targeting women attending an early morning workout class at a Madison fitness center, prosecutors said.

Madison and Rankin Counties District Attorney John K. “Bubba” Bramlett announced that Victor Andrew Ogiste, 29, and Ramone Davis, 31, both of Fort Lauderdale, Florida, were convicted in connection with a string of auto burglaries at Burn Boot Camp in Madison in October 2023.

Ogiste was sentenced to 35 years in the custody of the Mississippi Department of Corrections without the possibility of parole or early release after being sentenced as a habitual offender. Davis received a 40-year sentence with the possibility of parole.

According to investigators, Madison police responded Oct. 13, 2023, after multiple vehicles were burglarized during a 5 a.m. workout class at Burn Boot Camp. Officers said an individual smashed windows on 11 vehicles in about 20 minutes, stealing purses, wallets, credit cards and other personal items before fleeing in a 2022 Toyota RAV4.

Surveillance footage allowed officers to identify the vehicle and enter its tag number into a license plate reader system. Investigators later learned a similar burglary had occurred two days earlier at a Burn Boot Camp location in Oxford.

The investigation led officers to a rented Airbnb in Hattiesburg, where investigators from the Madison Police Department and Forrest County Sheriff’s Office executed search warrants and recovered stolen property from the Madison and Oxford burglaries, including credit cards, driver’s licenses and other personal belongings.

Authorities later tracked the suspects to Alabama after learning they were traveling in a Chrysler 300. Officers in Trussville conducted a traffic stop, identifying Ogiste as the driver and Davis as a passenger.

Investigators analyzed several cell phones recovered from the vehicle and found evidence placing both men at the Madison burglary scene. Prosecutors said Ogiste had searched online for Burn Boot Camp locations, and geolocation data showed both defendants traveling from Fort Lauderdale through multiple states before arriving in Mississippi.

Ogiste failed to appear for trial and was tried in absentia in September 2025. A Madison County jury convicted him on 11 counts of auto burglary and one count of conspiracy. U.S. Marshals later arrested him in Fort Worth, Texas, in December 2025.

Davis also failed to appear for court but was later arrested and pleaded guilty to five burglary counts and one count of conspiracy.

Bramlett praised the multi-agency investigation and said modern investigative tools, including GPS and cell phone data, played a major role in securing the convictions.

item.title: Donations pour in for Hattiesburg therapist after wife killed in Petal flash flooding - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
HATTIESBURG — Friends and supporters are rallying around a Hattiesburg family after a local therapist battling brain cancer lost his wife in a flash flood tragedy over Memorial Day weekend.

A GoFundMe created for Ben Floyd has seen an outpouring of support following the death of his wife, Rachael Floyd, who organizers say was killed May 25 during a flash flood incident in Petal.

The fundraiser was originally launched after Ben Floyd was diagnosed with a high-grade astrocytoma with piloid features, an aggressive form of brain cancer located in the cerebellum. Organizers said Floyd, who is self-employed as a therapist in Hattiesburg, has been unable to work regularly while undergoing treatment.

Following Rachael Floyd’s sudden death, organizers updated the fundraiser to state that donations will now help Ben Floyd care for the couple’s three young sons while navigating both his medical battle and the loss of his wife.

Supporters described Floyd as a compassionate counselor, devoted father and active member of the community who has spent years helping others through personal crises and hardships.

The couple’s children are Joshua, 4, Gilead, 2, and Mayhew, 1, according to the fundraiser page.

Organizers said additional information about funeral arrangements for Rachael Floyd is expected to be announced later.

item.title: UMMC AirCare expands fleet with addition of fixed-wing aircraft - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Special to Darkhorse Press
item.description:
By Rachel Vanderford University of Mississippi Medical Center

JACKSON – The University of Mississippi Medical Center AirCare flight team is preparing to expand its fleet with the addition of a fixed-wing aircraft and is looking to hire 10 additional medical staff members to support the new service.

The aircraft, a Pilatus PC-12 provided through UMMC’s partnership with Global Medical Response, will become the fifth vehicle in the AirCare fleet, expanding the program’s ability to provide in-state and regional patient transport.

“Adding a fixed-wing aircraft is a natural evolution for AirCare and gives us another tool to serve patients across Mississippi and the surrounding region,” said Jeremy Benson, director of the Mississippi Center for Emergency Services, and program director for AirCare – Helicopter Transport. “It allows us to move patients safely and efficiently over longer distances, particularly when rotor-wing transport may not be the most practical option.”

AirCare routinely receives transport requests involving patients who require specialized care not readily available in their local communities. The addition of a fixed-wing asset strengthens UMMC’s ability to support these missions across Mississippi and the surrounding region, including long-distance transports from neighboring states to UMMC’s Level I trauma center and other advanced specialty services.

“With highly specialized services such as stroke, transplant, trauma, neonatal, STEMI and burn care, UMMC serves as a critical referral destination for some of the sickest and most seriously injured patients in the region,” said Dr. Kendall McKenzie, chair of the Department of Emergency Medicine. “This additional transport capability enhances our emergency response network and helps ensure patients can be transferred safely and efficiently to the care teams and resources they need.”

“Often, we see patients who need access to a higher level of specialized care, and distance can become a real operational barrier,” Benson said. “This fixed-wing asset helps us bridge that gap. It gives AirCare the ability to reach farther, support our partner hospitals more effectively and bring patients to the right level of care in a safe, timely and efficient manner.”

The fixed-wing aircraft is configured to transport one patient while providing expanded cabin space for the medical crew, equipment and mission-specific supplies. Its increased range, carrying capacity and weather-capable features, enhance AirCare’s ability to safely complete longer-distance transports and operate in conditions that may limit rotor-wing aircraft.

GMR, which provides pilots, mechanics and aircraft for the AirCare fleet, will continue its partnership with UMMC as the fixed-wing program launches.

“We are proud to partner with the University of Mississippi Medical Center AirCare on the expansion of their flight program,” said Billy Casey, regional director of GMR. “This important addition strengthens their capacity to provide exceptional clinical care to communities across Mississippi and neighboring states.”

“This expansion reflects UMMC’s commitment to ensuring patients across Mississippi and the region have access to the highest level of care when and where they need it,” said Dr. Alan Jones, associate vice chancellor for health affairs. “The addition of a fixed-wing aircraft strengthens our ability to connect patients with specialized services more efficiently while supporting hospitals and communities that rely on the Medical Center for advanced care.”

AirCare is currently hiring for several positions to support the expansion of the flight program, including Flight Paramedic, Critical Care Paramedic and RN Flight / Transport roles. More information and application details are available on the UMMC Careers website.

item.title: Two Injured in Lauderdale County Shooting Investigation - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Greer Vari
item.description:

item.title: Two Baldwyn men arrested after deputies respond to burglary in progress - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
PRENTISS COUNTY – Two Baldwyn men were arrested after deputies responded to a burglary in progress at a Prentiss County home.

According to the Prentiss County Sheriff’s Office, deputies were dispatched around 9:34 a.m. May 22 to a residence at 20 County Road 5075.

Deputies Navarro and Lawson met with the homeowner’s sister, who said two men had forced their way into her brother’s home. She told deputies she saw the suspects on security camera footage and that both men ran into the woods behind the home when she arrived.

The suspects were described as shirtless, with one wearing black shorts and the other wearing brown pants.

Deputies spotted two people matching the description running along the property line. Both were taken into custody without incident and identified as 29-year-old Jacob Wayne Mears and 37-year-old Aaron Eddie Kelly, both of Baldwyn.

Deputies said a search of the suspects found multiple items belonging to the homeowner. A large amount of methamphetamine was also found near the suspects where they were taken into custody.

The homeowner told deputies items had also been removed from a disabled vehicle on the property and placed into a 2008 GMC Sierra registered to Mears. The truck was backed into the driveway with a trailer loaded with appliances, according to the sheriff’s office.

A .22 revolver found on the trailer was also recovered and identified by the homeowner as having been taken from under his bed.

Authorities said security camera images showed both suspects entering and leaving the residence.

Mears was charged with burglary of a dwelling, burglary of an automobile and possession of methamphetamine, 10 to 30 grams, enhanced with a firearm.

Kelly was charged with burglary of a dwelling, burglary of an automobile, possession of a weapon by a felon, possession of methamphetamine, 10 to 30 grams, enhanced with a firearm, and tampering with physical evidence. Authorities said all charges against Kelly will be pursued under habitual offender status.

Both suspects are currently under supervision by the Mississippi Department of Corrections, according to the sheriff’s office.

Justice Court Judge Ray Hall set Mears’ bond at $150,000 and Kelly’s bond at $200,000.

Both men were taken to the Prentiss County Jail. The charges will be presented to a Prentiss County grand jury.

item.author: Special to Darkhorse Press
item.description:
Ouachita Parish – The Louisiana State Police has issued a Silver Alert on behalf of the Monroe Police Department for 67-year-old Blanche Thomas McGhee.

She was discovered missing from her residence on Harrison Street today, at approximately 10:11 a.m. The Louisiana State Police received the request to issue a Silver Alert at approximately 1:49 p.m.

McGhee is a black female with brown eyes and black hair. She is 5’5” and weighs approximately 199 pounds. Family reports that McGhee has a medical condition that may impair her judgment.

McGhee is believed to be driving a silver 2018 Toyota RAV4 bearing Louisiana license plate 343JVI. Anyone with information regarding McGhee’s whereabouts is asked to immediately contact the Monroe Police Department at (318) 329-2600 or dial 911. All questions should be directed to the Monroe Police Department.

item.title: Senatobia Public Library to host local author festival June 6 - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
SENATOBIA — Readers will have a chance to meet Mississippi authors, purchase signed books and hear the stories behind their work during the upcoming Author Fest at the Senatobia Public Library on June 6.

The event will feature authors published through Rose & Pearl Publishing and showcase a variety of genres ranging from faith-based books and memoirs to children’s literature and Southern fiction.

Featured authors include Pat Hardison, author of “Facing the Fire”; Troy Day, author of “The Fruit”; Chilly Billy Howell, author of “Wrestling with Wisdom at the Crossroads”; and Heather Burchfield, author of “Not Here to Be Nice.”

Other featured works include “Floating Thoughts” by Candy Warren, “First Steps of Faith” by Carolyn Wiley and Candy Warren, and the children’s book “Who Am I When No One is Around?”

Organizers said the festival is intended to celebrate local storytelling and connect readers with authors from their own communities.

The event will take place June 6 at the Senatobia Public Library.

item.title: Pike County jury convicts McComb man on sexual battery charges involving child - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
PIKE COUNTY — A Pike County jury found a McComb man guilty Tuesday on charges of sexual battery and touching a child for lustful purposes following a one-day trial in Circuit Court.

According to prosecutors, Calvin Rasheed Patterson, 34, was convicted on one count of sexual battery and one count of touching and handling a child for lustful purposes.

The charges stemmed from an investigation launched after the victim came forward in 2024 and reported that Patterson assaulted her in July of that year. Prosecutors said the victim, now 15 years old, testified before the jury about the abuse.

Following the verdict, Circuit Judge Michael Taylor sentenced Patterson to 25 years in the custody of the Mississippi Department of Corrections to be served day for day. Patterson will also be required to register as a sex offender.

“I want to thank the McComb Police Department, and the nursing staff at Southwest Mississippi Regional Medical Center for all of their hard work and continuing investigation into such serious crimes. We continue to have young people come forward and describe the abuse that they have been subjected to. Our office will continue to work to protect our youth from predators that choose harm the most vulnerable of our community. Joey and Sebastian did an outstanding job and worked tirelessly to get justice for this young lady and hold Patterson accountable for his actions. I am proud of my team and how brave this young lady was in coming forward and sharing her story,” said District Attorney Brendon Adams.

Assistant District Attorneys Sebastian Harrell and Joey Norton prosecuted the case.

item.title: Mississippi seniors can apply for farmers market nutrition benefits - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
The Mississippi Department of Agriculture and Commerce is providing eligible senior citizens access to fresh, locally grown foods through the Senior Farmers Market Nutrition Program.

The program provides qualified seniors with a benefit card valued at $40. The card can be used at authorized farmers markets in 28 counties across Mississippi to purchase locally grown fruits, vegetables and honey.

MDAC said program information, including eligibility requirements and instructions on how to apply for and redeem the benefit card, is available on the Farmers Market Nutrition Program webpage at mdac.ms.gov.

Senior citizens who applied online and received benefits in the past must reapply online to receive benefits in 2026.

item.title: Mississippi Magnolia Gardens seeks donations to expand memorial tribute space - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON — A memorial garden at the Mississippi Agriculture and Forestry Museum is giving Mississippians a way to honor loved ones while helping preserve a decades-old tradition rooted in the state’s history.

The Mississippi Magnolia Gardens, located on the museum grounds in Jackson, allows donors to dedicate gifts in honor or memory of individuals and organizations through contributions supporting the garden’s continued growth and maintenance.

Officials with the Mississippi Agriculture and Forestry Museum Foundation said donations begin at $75 and help fund landscaping, plantings and long-term improvements to the garden space, which includes magnolia trees, walkways and gathering areas designed for reflection and remembrance.

The project continues the legacy of Mississippi’s former “Avenue of Magnolias,” a longtime statewide program that allowed families to honor loved ones through magnolia tree plantings. The current Magnolia Gardens opened in 2021, approximately 60 years after the original tradition began.

Foundation leaders said more than $100,000 in donations helped complete the initial phase of the gardens, but another $150,000 is needed to fully complete the planned vision for the site.

“The Mississippi Magnolia Gardens is more than a garden; it is a storybook of Mississippi families, memories, and milestones,” Foundation Board Chair Dr. Bill Herndon said. “Every donation helps ensure this tradition continues for generations to come.”

According to the foundation, each donation is acknowledged with a letter, and honorees or family members designated by donors also receive notification of the tribute.

The gardens are open year-round during regular museum hours.

Additional information and donation opportunities are available through the Mississippi Agriculture and Forestry Museum Foundation.
